1933.prule: Tone language (mora-based tone melodies; five verbal tone classes). 1933.tone: ǁAni is a tone language: Vossen (ed.) 2013 excerpt: 'In ǁAni, tonal behaviour appears to comply with the mora principle; i.e., at least two tonal segments – High and/or...' with melodies LH, L-H, H-L, H-M, H-H, MH-M, MH-H, H-M-M; WALS 13A codes it 'simple tone system' (Vossen 1986, 1997). On stress: Heine 1999 finds stress but says its 'exact significance is unclear'; Vossen 2003 treats stress as 'a distinctive unit... inherent even to the citation form of the verb', perceptible 'in most cases', located on the last H-tone syllable of the verbal stem (tone classes 2/3/5) or shifted to the juncture morpheme (classes 1/4); Downing 2010 summarises: 'stress is assigned to the last High-toned syllable of verbs... all lexical morphemes appear to be assigned stress', with exceptions. Körtvélyessy & Štekauer (eds.) 2024 excerpt: 'Stress does not appear to be a relevant category in languages of the Khoe-Kwadi family (however, see Vossen 2003 on ǁAni)'. Stress placement is therefore derived from tone, not from syllable count or weight.

1933.cfw: ǁAni is a tone language on every account (Vossen 2003; WALS after Vossen 1986 and 1997; Downing 2004), and the two field descriptions of its verbal stress, Heine 1999 and Vossen 2003, both put it on the last high-toned syllable of the verb and differ only in detail (Heine's preceding-low-tone condition and his doubt about its significance; Vossen's finding that it is inherent to tone classes 2, 3 and 5 and shifts to the juncture morpheme in classes 1 and 4), so the record rests on few sources but faces no real dissent.

1934.dq: The following account is preliminary only and restricted to stress in isolated word forms. In connected discourse the stress patterns may be different due to higher-level targets. ... • The penultimate syllable of words is the primary stress target (Stokes 1981; Leeding 1989)
1934.dloc: Ch. 2 'Segmental phonology and phonotactics', section 2.4 'Stress', p. 27 (chapter p. 12).
1934.heavy: Heavy syllables attract stress, where syllable weight is determined by the number of morae. Long vowels, diphthongs and closed syllables are bimoraic and are stress attractors. (The 'long vowels' are /a/ and /ɛ/, which 'tend to be longer than the other vowels' /i, ə/; the language has no phonemic length contrast.)
1934.prule: Primary stress targets the penultimate syllable, but the system is quantity-sensitive: heavy (bimoraic) syllables - long vowels (the inherently longer /a/ and /ɛ/), diphthongs and closed syllables - attract stress, so stress may shift to the antepenult when the antepenult is heavy and the penult holds /i/ or /ə/; when the two principles compete stress varies (e.g. akina [ˈakəna ~ aˈkina]); epenthetic vowels are never stressed, even in the penult; final syllables are not stressed (Stokes 1981: 157 'never falls on the final syllable'; Leeding 1989: 142 excepts the suffixes -aki, -tha).
1934.srule: van Egmond 2012 states no general rule for secondary stress: 'The pronominal prefixes on verbs generally receive secondary stress' (prefixes 'have secondary stress'), and her transcriptions mark a secondary stress on the first syllable of 4-5-syllable words ([ˌmakaˈʈuwa], [ˌawaɾuˈwaʎa], [ˌɛɾiˈpɛɾipa]), once on the second ([jiˌpiʎiˈpiʎa]). Placement per Leeding 1989 (Umbakumba): besides the penultimate primary, stress falls on the first syllable; even-syllabled words stress alternate syllables, the first of each disyllabic foot (1010, 101010); longer odd-syllabled words keep initial + penultimate stress with a trisyllabic first foot, then disyllabic feet (10010, 1001010); trisyllables usually penult only. Stokes 1981 (Angurugu): in four-syllable words 'the first and penultimate vowels are stressed'.
1934.quote: The rules for assigning stress are complex, and there is a lot of variation, resulting from several competing factors that determine stress. There is a general penultimate stress target, but, as in other Arnhem Land languages (Baker 2008a), stress is also quantity-sensitive ... The vowels /a/ and /ɛ/ tend to be longer than the other vowels ..., so they attract the stress and possibly disturb the general pattern of penultimate stress assignment. Closed syllables are also heavy and likewise attract stress. ... The following account is preliminary only and restricted to stress in isolated word f…

1934.tone: No tone. Stress realised by 'a combination of pitch and amplitude' (van Egmond 2012: 27); Leeding 1989: 139: 'A stressed syllable differs from an unstressed by a slight increase in intensity and length and a very slight rise in pitch. (Stress might better be defined as syllable prominence.)' Leeding also describes a length + very-high-pitch stylistic feature on the penult of verbs for continuity of action (not lexical tone).

1938.prule: Word stress falls on the penultimate or the final syllable depending on the word, i.e. lexically/morphologically fixed within a right-edge two-syllable window (desenfáixa 3sg.pres. vs desenfaixár inf.; both are vowel-final in Chistabino because final /r/ is silent, so the position is not recoverable from the final segment). Antepenultimate stress is marginal (hypercorrect forms like pántano; per EFA 2017 toponyms; per AAL 2023 some verb forms, toponyms and the Ansó variety) and modern Aragonese regularises proparoxytones to paroxytones. No weight or syllable-count rule is stated.
1938.srule: Not mentioned by Mott 2007 ('Prosody': Lexical stress, Rhythm, Intonation, pp. 110-111). For common Aragonese only a morphologically conditioned secondary accent is described: adverbs in -ment are final-stressed and may carry a secondary accent on the lexeme (malament, comunment, regularment; AAL 2023 sec. 3.5c; EFA 2017 sec. 19.4.1 malament, tasament), and some prefixes may generate one (antisocial [ˌan̪tisoˈθjal], EFA 2017 sec. 19.4.1). No rhythmic secondary stress is described; polysyllabic words have one tonic syllable (EFA 2017 sec. 1.2.1.1).

1943.prule: Stress position is set by word class and morphological structure, not by a single quantity-insensitive or weight-based position: verb forms carry primary stress on the first syllable of the verb root (secondary stress on the subject-pronoun prefix; template pro + tns + verb root, e.g. [ya + tak + ni.aw] 'I see' with root-initial stress); three-syllable non-verbs stress the second syllable ([mu.lu.al] 'wallaby', [ko.ko.lek] 'bad'); two-syllable nouns usually stress the first syllable ([ta.kal] 'bushknife'), two-syllable modifiers usually the second ([te.ken] 'long'); reduplicated noun stems always first ([sal.sal] 'broom'), reduplicated modifier stems always second ([tek.tek] 'early'). Stressed syllables are marked by underlining in the manuscript examples.
1943.srule: Verb forms only: secondary stress on the subject-pronoun prefix, primary stress on the first syllable of the verb root (template pro + tns + verb rt: [ya + tak + ni.aw] 'I see', [e + naw + kum] 'you will buy', [yi + aw + mèn.i.u] 'he is sitting down', [om + ka + mo.'o] 'you (pl) sang'). No secondary or rhythmic stress is described for nouns, modifiers or other non-verb words; the 1992 OPD does not repeat the statement.

1945.prule: Sesquisyllabic/iambic word template: an optional unstressed minor syllable (C + brief schwa, no coda, no tone) followed by the stressed major (full) syllable; minor syllables can never be word-final, so prominence is on the final (major) syllable of the (minor)+major word: 'Asho Chin has an iambic stress pattern'; Butler's 'word-final prosodic prominence' analysis of sesquisyllables adopted for Asho. Monosyllables (major) trivially stressed. In compounds of two monosyllabic morphemes the first member may undergo iambic weakening to a minor syllable in fast/casual speech. Stress is described alongside a two-tone (H/L) system; tone is carried only by stressed (major) syllables.

1946.prule: No general word-stress rule is stated for Āštīāni. What the sources give is a suffix-conditioned pattern in nouns: the singular feminine marker -a and the definite direct-case endings -i (masc.) / -o (fem.) are unstressed (Yarshater: 'The fem. marker is an unstressed –a', 'unstressed –i for masc. sing.... –o for fem. sing.'), so feminine -a nouns carry penultimate stress (úa 'water', várfa 'snow', kúa 'cat', xúa 'shovel', sía 'apple', kárga 'hen', kāláka 'melon', esbéza 'louse', detáka 'daughter', bóza 'the goat') while masculine nouns ending in -a carry final stress (kiá/kiyá 'house', esbá 'dog'); Tafazzoli states this explicitly as a masculine/feminine contrast ('in masculine words ending in a the stress is on the last syllable'). Yarshater's other accent-marked forms (Hasán, púl-i, bóz-o, zenía, bāˊla) are consistent with stress on the last syllable of the stem before these unstressed endings, but that stem-final generalisation is an inference from citation forms, not a sentence in either source. Position in a word is therefore decided by suffix identity, not by syllable count (úa f. vs kiá m., both two syllables). Nothing on verbs, secondary stress or syllable weight.

1947.prule: No general word-stress rule is stated. Beltrame marks 'la posa della voce' vowel by vowel with three accent signs that simultaneously encode vowel quality and length (acute = close short, grave = open short, circumflex = open long) and writes them only 'where necessary'; several words carry two marks (kòbè p. 29; nèndì, nèndé p. 625), so a mark does not single out one prominent vowel. The citation forms of the (bisyllabic k-CV) verbs on p. 29 all bear a final-vowel mark (read on drops several). The only generalisations are three morphological statements for verbs: in the se- present the accent 'ordinarily' moves from the last to the first vowel (kognò > se-mògno); in the imperative the last vowel is pronounced with emphasis (kojó emé); before postposed negative ka the accent is carried on the last syllable of the verb (mognò-ka). Nouns receive no statement (vocabulary: 303 final-marked vs 110 penultimate-marked tokens, 43 multi-marked, an earlier compilation tally, scan noise included). Whether the marked prominence is stress or tone heard as stress cannot be decided from this 1870s amateur description of a Mangbetuic (tonal) language.

tn.quote: Tone is a prominent feature of all Lakes Plain languages and therefore was most likely a feature of some of the protolanguages as well. ... All the modem languages have at least high and low tone. Duvle and Sikaritai have only these tones with Martin (1991) analysing the Sikaritai system as pitch-accent. The remainder of the languages also have combinations of high and low (or contours) ... [p.160] Although tonal contrast is found in virtually all of the the Lakes Plain languages, it will not be shown in the word list transcriptions.

1959.prule: Primary stress on the first syllable of the word; stated without reference to syllable weight, vowel quality or morphology (fixed initial).
1959.srule: Secondary stress exists but no placement rule is given: Hoenigman 2015 (App. A sec. 1.1.3) says each vowel of a true vowel sequence is a separate syllable carrying its own stress, and the one stress-marked example, disyllabic [wá·i·] <wai> 'wind; string bag', has primary stress on the first and secondary stress on the second syllable. Secondary stress in longer words or words without vowel sequences is not described; not mentioned in the Hoenigman 2025 chapter abstract.

affix_stress.q: Awiakay has twelve consonants and twelve vowels, primary stress occurs on the first syllable. Verbs are inflected for person and number of subject and object arguments, as well as TAM. Nouns take case marking and may be marked for possession.
